name: msitools
why: Lets you inspect and extract Windows MSI installer databases on a Mac, a real file-format door.

brief.what_it_is: msitools is a set of command-line programs for inspecting and building Windows Installer (.MSI) packages. The inspection tools (msiinfo, msidump, msiextract, msidiff) take an existing MSI file and show its tables, streams, and embedded files, or extract the files, or diff two packages. The build tools (msibuild, a low-level builder, and wixl, a WiX-like builder) take MSI tables or an XML description and produce an MSI file. wixl-heat builds XML fragments from a list of files and directories. The wiki also notes that osslsigncode 1.5.1 or later can sign the resulting MSI files.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says msitools is meant to be a solution for packaging and deploying cross-compiled Windows applications. It is built on libmsi, a portable library for reading and writing MSI files, which is itself a port of a subset of Wine's Windows Installer implementation.
brief.how_it_works: libmsi does the reading and writing of MSI files, and the command-line tools sit on top of it. The README says MSI files are OLE Structured Storage files, and msitools uses libgsf to read that container format. wixl parses an XML document and tries to use the same syntax as the WiX toolset.
brief.install_notes: The brew formula is the only install path the README mentions. The wiki says release tarballs are at https://download.gnome.org/sources/msitools/. Nothing beyond the normal build dependencies (libgsf is one) is mentioned, and I saw no first-run configuration.
brief.standout: wixl tries to accept the same XML syntax as Microsoft's WiX toolset, so you can build Windows installers on macOS or Linux without the Windows toolchain. The inspection tools also let you open and extract MSI files, which is a file-format look that most people never get.
brief.status: Unknown to slightly quiet. The GNOME wiki page carries a 2024-10-23 timestamp, but it now displays a notice that the site has been retired and points to handbook.gnome.org and gitlab.gnome.org. The README is from the GitLab project and I saw no release date or last-commit date in either page, so I cannot confirm current maintenance.
brief.caveats: The README says msitools does not work under Windows and is planned to self-host later. It also says the project is in a very early stage, though usable. The README and wiki both say wixl lacks many features compared with WiX. The homepage in the brew formula is a retired wiki, so some links may be stale. Signing needs a separate tool, osslsigncode. I did not check the license.
quotes: msitools is a set of programs to inspect and build Windows Installer (.MSI) files.
While in a very early stage, it is already usable.
Wixl lacks many features compared to WiX. As always, contributions are welcome!
fetch_log: https://wiki.gnome.org/msitools: worked, but the page is a retired-site archive notice with the project text and links
https://github.com/GNOME/msitools: worked, returned the README (the GitHub URL redirects to the GNOME GitLab project; no separate docs were fetched)

judge.reason: A cross-platform toolkit for opening MSI’s database-like internals and building Windows installers without Windows is a worthwhile, under-the-radar file-format detour.

entry.title: msitools
entry.tldr: Open, dump, diff and extract Windows .MSI installers from a Mac or Linux terminal, or build new ones from XML without Windows.
entry.deeper_look:
msitools is a set of command-line programs for inspecting and building Windows Installer (.MSI) packages. The inspection side takes an existing MSI and shows its tables and streams (`msiinfo`, `msidump`), pulls out the embedded files (`msiextract`), or compares two packages (`msidiff`).

The build side goes the other way. `msibuild` is a low-level builder that works from MSI tables. `wixl` reads an XML description and writes an MSI, and tries to use the same syntax as Microsoft's WiX toolset. `wixl-heat` generates XML fragments from a list of files and directories. The README says the point is packaging and deploying cross-compiled Windows applications.

Underneath is libmsi, a portable library for reading and writing MSI files, itself a port of a subset of Wine's Windows Installer implementation. The README explains that an MSI is an OLE Structured Storage file, a container format msitools reads through libgsf. That makes an installer a small database of tables with files packed alongside, rather than an opaque executable. Most people never see inside one.

try_this.what_happens: Lists what the inspection tool can show about an MSI file, such as its tables and streams.
Shows how to unpack the files embedded in an MSI without running the installer.
Shows the options for building an MSI from a WiX-style XML file.

entry.whats_unique: wixl accepts WiX-style XML, so Windows installers can be built on macOS or Linux without the Windows toolchain. The inspection tools open up a file format most people only ever double-click.
entry.caveats: The README calls the project very early stage though usable, says wixl lacks many WiX features, and the homepage is a retired GNOME wiki, so current maintenance is unclear.
